name: Riddim-inspired half-time flow
rules: Keep tempo and meter unchanged.
Preserve pitches for rhythm-only transformations.
Use a half-time backbeat with snare on beat 3 in 4/4.
Shorten or reposition existing bass notes to make motifs with deliberate rests, without adding notes.
Use offbeat and triplet placements as variations, not on every note.
Leave space for pad stabs and fills.
variation: Create subtle and strong variants; vary every 2 or 4 bars.
notes: Initial heuristic for first MVP milestone; human listening tests required.

name: Sustained pad chord foundation
rules: Hold chord tones for most of the bar.
Use sparse offbeat chord stabs as a variation.
Do not alter pitch content in rhythm-only edits.

name: 7/8 groove in 2+2+3
summary: Mark an uneven meter by spacing three accents across the bar rather than moving the 4/4 backbeat unchanged.
rules: In this example, accent offsets 0, 1 and 2 quarter-note beats within a 3.5-beat bar.
Try kick at 0 and 1, snare at 2, and lighter existing hi-hats at 0.5, 1.5, 2.5 or 3 as available.
Keep the first bass attack clear and let the longer final group create space before the next bar.
notes: A sketchpad example, not a universal 7/8 grouping. For rhythm-only edits, move existing notes only.

name: Kick and bass attack spacing
summary: Separate some kick and bass attacks with a short rhythmic gap to make both easier to hear.
grid_suggestions: Try a 0.25 or 0.5 quarter-note beat offset
rules: Keep the kick as the reference; try delaying an existing bass attack after a kick and shorten it if needed to keep the next note clear.
Keep other shared attacks where a strong downbeat is useful. Compare with the original at the same tempo.
notes: This is an arrangement choice, not sidechain compression. Results depend on the intended groove.

name: Syncopation / anticipation in chord attacks
rules: Move selected chord attacks slightly before or after the expected beat rather than shifting every chord.
Use half-beat anticipation as a starting example, then listen against the drum groove.
Keep other chord hits on the beat so the syncopated attacks have contrast.

source.title: おしゃれコード進行一覧 — ジャンル別の解説
source.author: SRM.

notes: SRM explicitly describes moving chord attacks before/after the beat; this record turns that explanation into a conservative MIDI-editing procedure.

name: Polyrhythmic chord-change cycle
rules: Keep the meter fixed while allowing chord changes to follow a different repeating cycle.
Do not change every track at once; begin with Pad chord-change positions.
Choose a cycle that eventually realigns with the bar grid, and mark the realignment point.
grid_suggestions: 3-quarter-note chord-change cycle over 4/4; test alignment after 3 bars

source.title: おしゃれコード進行一覧 — ジャンル別の解説
source.author: SRM.

notes: SRM describes changing chord timing in a 3-beat cycle against 4/4 to create a polyrhythmic effect, then realigning it with the bar. The exact source diagram should be checked before reproducing a specific note pattern.

name: Stop-time chord hits
rules: Create a coordinated hit on a chosen accent, then leave a deliberate gap.
Let the next bass or drum attack restart the groove rather than filling every subdivision.
Use sparingly at section boundaries or as a drop variation.

source.title: おしゃれコード進行一覧 — ジャンル別の解説
source.author: SRM.

notes: SRM defines stop-time as coordinated 'kime' hits and links chord changes to those hits.

name: Harmonic rhythm follows phrase density
rules: Longer melodic phrases can sit over longer chord holds.
For faster or denser sections, try shorter chord durations or a two-beat harmonic rhythm.
Short inserted chords such as subV or ii–V should usually be shorter than the target chord they approach.
grid_suggestions: 1 beat for passing ii or V

source.title: おしゃれコード進行一覧 — ジャンル別の解説
source.author: SRM.

notes: Paraphrases SRM's harmonic-rhythm discussion; adjust by listening rather than treating tempo as the only factor.

name: Conservative microtiming
rules: Do not add random timing offsets to every note.
Compare the straight version with small, track-specific timing changes.
Avoid exaggerating microtiming; the cited jazz study found expanded deviations reduced swing ratings relative to the original performances.
Treat swing ratio and tempo as separate parameters.
grid_suggestions: test subtle offsets only on selected voices

source.title: Microtiming Deviations and Swing Feel in Jazz
source.author: George Datseris et al.

notes: The source studies jazz swing, not Riddim. Apply the general caution against exaggerated offsets, but do not transfer jazz timing values as a Riddim recipe.

name: Groove and microtiming research overview
rules: Treat groove as more than a swing ratio: timing deviations, rhythmic pattern and body-movement response are studied together.
When designing a transformation, record which track is moved and by how much so candidates can be compared.
grid_suggestions: record onset offsets in milliseconds and beat fractions

source.title: マイクロタイミングに着目したグルーヴ研究の展望
source.author: 惠谷隆英・三浦哲都・河瀬諭・工藤和俊・藤井進也

notes: Japanese-language review article surveying psychological research on microtiming and groove; it is a research overview, not a genre-specific MIDI pattern.

name: Riddim drop flow — producer tutorial reference
rules: Study the drum groove, bass placement and drop arrangement as separate layers.
Transcribe the actual note placements from the tutorial before treating them as a reusable MIDI pattern.
Do not assume one universal Riddim pattern; compare multiple examples.

source.title: How To FLOW & SONG ARRANGEMENT (BASS Music/DUBSTEP)
source.author: Dripment

notes: The creator describes the video as a lesson on rhythm in drops, song arrangement and creating flow in dubstep/tearout. No exact MIDI pattern has been transcribed here.

name: Riddim drop layer study: drums, synth flow and sub bass
rules: Study the drum pattern first, then the synth-flow role, then the sub-bass role.
Keep the rhythmic role of each layer distinct when adapting the groove to a three-track sketch.
Treat sound-design demonstrations separately from MIDI timing instructions.

source.title: How to RIDDIM — Dubstep Tutorial by Dack Janiels
source.author: Dack Janiels / Avant Samples

notes: The chapter list separates Drums (0:51–1:59), Synths & Flow (2:00–2:46) and Sub Bass (4:25–5:37). The database records the lesson structure, not a copied project or sample.

name: Chord emotion and drum-break contribution to groove
rules: When comparing groove candidates, test the chord progression with and without the drum pattern.
Do not attribute a groove change to harmony alone; the study evaluates chord progression characteristics together with rhythmic accompaniment.

source.title: Is happier music groovier? The influence of emotional characteristics of musical chord progressions on groove
source.author: Satoshi Kawase

notes: Study-specific finding: drum-break accompaniment increased groove ratings for both happy and sad progressions; happier progressions were more likely to elicit groove in the tested stimuli. Not a genre rule.

name: Straight pop backbeat
rules: Keep the main pulse straight; do not apply swing globally.
Use a clear kick foundation and snare backbeat, with hi-hat subdivisions carrying motion.
Create interest with pickups, rests and occasional offbeat chord stabs rather than constant fills.
variation: Change one layer at a time; keep the backbeat recognizable.
notes: Starter arrangement heuristic for the app; not a transcription of a particular recording.

name: Selective triplet shuffle
rules: Use a long-short subdivision based on triplets for selected voices.
Do not swing every track by the same amount; let kick and snare anchor the pulse while hats, bass or chord attacks provide the shuffle.
Mix straight attacks with shuffled responses so the groove can breathe.
variation: Apply the shuffle to one or two layers first, then compare a stronger version.
notes: General shuffle-arrangement heuristic. Swing ratios vary by genre, performance and tempo.

name: Half-time backbeat
rules: In 4/4, place the principal snare or clap on beat 3 to create a half-time backbeat.
Keep the actual BPM unchanged; create the slower feel through backbeat placement and note density.
Use kick syncopation and short fills to connect phrases.
variation: Keep the snare anchor stable while varying kick and bass placements.
notes: Basic half-time arrangement concept; exact patterns depend on style.

name: Syncopated breakbeat
rules: Use syncopated kick and snare placements rather than a uniform four-on-the-floor pulse.
Create a recognizable one- or two-bar motif, then vary only selected hits at phrase endings.
Let hi-hat subdivisions and bass pickups answer the main drum accents.
variation: Use a stable core loop with small two-bar and four-bar changes.
notes: Starter breakbeat arrangement heuristic; not tied to a single breakbeat subgenre.

name: Sixteenth-note funk pocket
rules: Use a 1/16 grid as a placement reference, not as a requirement to fill every slot.
Build the pocket from short notes, rests and accents around the kick/snare relationship.
Allow bass and chord stabs to answer one another; avoid making all parts equally busy.
variation: Keep the main groove stable and vary one pickup or response per two bars.
notes: General funk-inspired MIDI heuristic; humanize and adjust by ear.

name: Displaced-accent math-rock pulse
rules: Keep the chosen meter stable while placing accents in repeating groups that cross the beat grouping.
Use a short repeating cell such as 3+3+2 eighth-note accents over 4/4.
Keep the bass part playable and let Pad attacks reinforce only selected accents.
variation: Return to a clear downbeat every two or four bars so the listener can reorient.
notes: A compositional starting point for displaced accents, not a definition of all math rock.
